draft.title: Galvanic cells
card: A galvanic cell splits a redox reaction into two half-cells. Electrons move through an external wire, so the reaction produces an electric current.
the electrode where oxidation happens. It is the negative terminal. Electrons leave the cell from here.
the electrode where reduction happens. It is the positive terminal. Electrons arrive here from the wire.
A salt bridge joins the two solutions, and ions move through it to balance charge. Cell voltage = E° of the cathode minus E° of the anode, and the half-cell with the higher E° is the cathode.
draft.remember: Oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode. Electrons flow through the wire, ions through the salt bridge.

a.q: In a working galvanic cell, which direction do electrons move in the external wire?
opts: From the anode to the cathode
From the cathode to the anode
From the salt bridge to the anode
From the cathode to the salt bridge
a.why: Oxidation at the anode releases electrons, and they travel through the wire to the cathode, where reduction uses them. Electrons do not pass through the salt bridge, which carries ions only.
a.clue: Electrons are released where oxidation happens.

b.q: A cell joins a zinc half-cell (E° = -0.76 V) to a copper half-cell (E° = +0.34 V). What is the cell voltage, and which is the anode?
opts: 1.10 V, and zinc is the anode
1.10 V, and copper is the anode
0.42 V, and zinc is the anode
0.42 V, and copper is the anode
b.why: The copper half-cell has the higher E°, so it is the cathode and zinc is the anode. Voltage = +0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10 V. Adding or mixing up the signs gives the tempting 0.42 V.
b.clue: The higher E° is the cathode. Subtract the anode's E° from it.

a.best: From the anode to the cathode

b.best: 1.10 V, and zinc is the anode
